title: Constitutional Law
description: This course is part of the required first-year JD curriculum. This course offers an introduction to American constitutional law. In addition to examining questions of interpretive method, the course focuses on the powers of the federal government and the allocation of decision making authority among government institutions, including both federalism and separation of powers. Class participation, attendance, written assignments, and final exam. This course is open to first-year Law School students only.

title: Contracts
description: This course is part of the required first-year JD curriculum. It provides exposure to basic contract law. The course will identify the scope and purpose of the legal protection accorded to interests predicated on contract and will focus on problems of contract formation, interpretation, performance, and remedies for breach.

title: Criminal Law
description: This course is part of the required first-year JD curriculum. It examines the traditional general issues in the substantive criminal law, including the purposes of punishment and the appropriate limits on the use of the criminal sanction. It focuses predominantly on how criminal statutes are organized around objective offense elements (conduct, causation, and attendant circumstances) and mental states, and to a lesser degree on inchoate crimes, complicity, justification and excuse.

title: Property
description: This course is part of the required first-year JD curriculum. It deals with possession and ownership of land and with the incidents thereof, including private and public restrictions on its use and development, nuisance, trespass, concurrent interests, landlord and tenant, and eminent domain. Attendance and final exam. Your instructor will advise you of other basis of grading. This course is open to first-year Law School students only.

title: Legal Writing
description: This course introduces students to the ways lawyers write to persuade. In a hypothetical criminal case in state court, students draw on the useful facts from the record, synthesize rules from cases, and analogize and distinguish cases in a closed universe. Students receive feedback from the instructor on multiple drafts before submission. Students then submit one persuasive brief on a motion in the conventions of the Bluebook. This course depends on participation; attendance is mandatory. Grading reflects written work, class preparedness and participation, and professionalism. This course is part of the required first-year JD curriculum.

title: Torts
description: This course is part of the required first-year JD curriculum. It considers issues involved in determining whether the law should require a person to compensate for harm intentionally or unintentionally caused. These problems arise in situations as diverse as automobile collisions, operations of nuclear facilities, and consumption of defective food products. Among other considerations, the course explores various resolutions in terms of their social, economic, and political implications.

title: Federal Litigation in a Global Context: Coursework
description: This course builds on the writing skills developed in Legal Writing. Students submit and orally argue one persuasive brief on a motion in federal district court. Students represent the plaintiff or defendant in a simulated global torts case that raises complex issues of federal civil procedure. Students work in an open universe with the online legal research tools, bluebook the cases, plan litigation strategy, peer review drafts, and moot a motion. This course depends on participation; attendance is mandatory. Winter grading reflects students' written work, including outlines, drafts, final briefs, citation, and professionalism. This course is open to first-year JD students only.

title: Federal Litigation in a Global Context: Methods and Practice
description: This course continues with the winter simulation with students representing the plaintiff or defendant in a global torts case. Students submit and orally argue one persuasive brief on a motion in federal district court. Students build on their writing and oral advocacy skills with more emphasis on the lawyering practice. Students lead strategy sessions, conduct legal writing by email, meet and confer with opposing counsel, research, bluebook, peer edit, moot, judge, and orally argue a motion. This course depends on participation; attendance is mandatory. Spring grading reflects all non-written aspects of the work, including research, strategy, peer review, moots, and oral argument (including your roles as a judge and colleague), and professionalism. This course is open to first-year JD students only.

title: Discussion (1L): Criminal Legal Histories
description: This discussion seminar will trace the roots of four critical aspects of the American criminal legal system: jury independence and the power of jurors to render verdicts according to conscience; plea bargaining and the marginalization of juries; penitentiaries and the displacement of other forms of punishment; and the criminalization of recreational drugs. Though modern criminal justice policy will inform our conversation, the readings will be historical with an emphasis on primary source documents. We will examine the forces driving legal evolution and the historian's tools in mapping those forces. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 6:30 PM-8:30 PM on Sept. 23, Oct. 7, Oct. 21, Nov 4.

title: Discussion (1L): Religion and the Profession of Law
description: This discussion seminar will focus on the interplay between religious identity, community, and worldview, and the study and practice of law. As a defining force for so many across the globe, and in the norms through which people anchor rights and relationships, religion has a unique and abiding impact on the legal profession -- for believer and nonbeliever alike. Whether as law students or seasoned practitioners, the need to anticipate, appreciate, and reconcile religious perspectives is both a vital skill and a resource for understanding and mutual respect. The class will meet across three campus sessions and a closing offsite dinner. It will involve a collaborative exploration of primary and secondary sources, as well as custom conversations. Topics will include religion and cross-cultural lawyering, religion and legal systems, faith in judicial decision-making, and law as a vocation. Befitting the goals of the discussion series and the importance of bridge-building, this seminar is warmly and equally open to students of any religious tradition and those of no religion at all. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 4:30 PM-6:30 PM on Oct. 8, Oct. 22, Nov. 5, Nov 19.

title: Discussion (1L): Representations of Criminal Lawyers in Popular Culture Through the Lens of Bias
description: This seminar will explore the portrayal of criminal lawyers in popular films and will engage in critical analysis of how misconceptions about the criminal justice system and biases against women, people of color and the poor are amplified on the big screen. Source materials will include numerous mass-market films juxtaposed against authoritative law review and other commentary to afford in-depth discussion. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 6:00 PM-8:00 PM on Sept. 24, Oct. 8, Oct. 22, Nov. 5.

title: Discussion (1L): Human Reproduction in the 21st Century
description: This group will discuss human reproduction in the remaining three quarters of the 21st century, with a glance back at its first quarter and at the 20th. We will talk about ethical, legal, and social issues arising from abortion, the moral and legal status of human embryos and fetuses, eugenics, embryo selection, embryo editing, ectogenesis, "depopulation," and more. An underlying theme will be how "we" -- as a culture, as a legal system, as legal systems, and as individuals -- decide what should and shouldn't be done. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 7:00 PM-9:00 PM on Sept. 28, Oct. 19, Oct. 26, Nov 9.

title: Discussion (1L): Race, Technology, and Law
description: We tend to think of technology as value neutral, as a set of essentially objective tools that people use, sometimes for good, sometimes for bad, particularly when questions of race and racial justice are involved. But are the technologies we develop and deploy really neutral? Or might they be shaped by historical prejudices, biases, and social inequalities? To what extent is technology perhaps no less biased and racist than the underlying society in which it exists? We will consider these questions and more in the context of a wide range of technologies, including risk assessment algorithms for bail, predictive policing, and other decisions in the criminal justice system; facial recognition systems; surveillance tools; algorithms for medical diagnosis and treatment decisions; targeted online housing ads that result in "digital redlining;" programs that determine entitlement to credit or public benefits and/or purport to detect fraud by recipients; algorithms used in recruiting and hiring; social-media targeting and disinformation; digital divide access gaps; and more. We will seek to articulate a framework for understanding how bias in tech might occur and how it might be related to racism and discrimination more broadly in our society. Finally, we will explore how these problems might be addressed, including by regulators, legislators, and courts as well as by technology developers and educators. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 4:30 PM-6:30 PM on Sept. 17, Oct. 1, Oct. 15, Oct. 29.

title: Discussion (1L): Rebuilding Civil Society from the Local to the National
description: Since America's founding, local political engagement (through participation, leadership, and organizing in local politics) has been a linchpin of our democratic order and adult education. That engagement is deeply challenged today by economic segregation, technological and media changes, the downsizing of local journalism, and the loss of institutions that forge local social networks (such as small businesses, churches, and neighborhood-based nonprofits). Yet meanwhile, poor and working class communities need local solutions and activism to face severe challenges such as environmental disasters, low wages, drug addiction, family dissolution, and disinvestment in basic services, schools, and infrastructure. This reading group will sit with stories and strategies of local democratic reengagement. Through a range of readings (from memoir to academic commentary) as well as films and podcasts, we'll discuss a deliberately diverse set of voices, from environmental activists to conservative thought leaders. We'll situate our discussions in a mix of urban and rural places, including California's agricultural interior, Oregon's timber counties, post-industrial Rust Belt cities, and urban and rural Mississippi. Our hope is that our group of students - like the authors and protagonists of our discussions -- will be racially, politically, economically, and geographically heterogeneous, allowing us to become better actors in the project of local political engagement for the public good. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 5:00 PM-7:00 PM on Sept. 16, Sept. 30, Oct. 14, Oct. 28.

title: Discussion (1L): What Makes a Great Judicial Opinion?
description: In law school, you will be reading a lot of judicial opinions. Most of the time, you'll be reading them with an eye to their legal holding. In this seminar, you'll be reading them with a different question in mind: What makes one judicial opinion better than another? What is it about certain opinions that leads them to be considered particularly effective or important? When is a judicial opinion "great"? You will read a variety of opinions from different judges and justices, subject areas, perspectives, and time periods, as well as some academic articles about judicial opinions and legal writing. Spoilers: There is no one answer to the title of this seminar. The goal will be to complicate the question and think about the different tools and objectives judges have when they write. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 5:00 PM-7:00 PM on Sept. 29, Oct. 13, Oct. 27, Nov 10.

title: Discussion (1L): Introduction to Election Law
description: This discussion seminar is intended to give students a basic understanding of the themes in the legal regulation of elections and politics. We will cover several Supreme Court cases on topics of voting rights, reapportionment/ redistricting, ballot access, regulation of political parties, and campaign finance. We will begin each session with an update on litigation related to the 2026 election and attempt to tie the themes of the class to ongoing controversies in the law of contemporary American democracy. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active prticipation. Class meets: 6:30 PM-8:30 PM on Sept. 29, Oct. 6, Oct. 13, Oct. 20.

title: Discussion (1L): What is the Rule of Law?
description: The "rule of law" is widely perceived to be under serious attack today, but what is the rule of law? Why does it matter, how should it be protected, and what connection does it have with democracy? This seminar will read perspectives on these questions from a range of legal scholars and judges, stretching from the mid- twentieth century to today. Our main goal will not be to decide who we think is right, or which arguments we find most congenial. Instead, we will try to understand the thinking on various sides of these controversies, and to see what value, if any, we can find even in the arguments we disagree with. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 5:00 PM-7:00 PM on Sept. 24, Oct. 8, Oct. 22, Nov 12.

title: Discussion (1L): AI tools for Legal Practice
description: Students in this discussion seminar will be introduced to various legal tools for AI practice. We will learn how to use Harvey, Claude for Legal, and other AI tools to perform basic tasks related to legal research, writing, and analysis. Each week students will be expected to experiment with one of these tools and to generate original work product. This will be taught jointly with one or more Stanford librarians. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 4:15 PM-6:15 PM on Sept. 29, Oct. 6, Oct. 13, Oct. 20.

title: Discussion (1L): American Identity, Pluralism, and Multiracial Democracy
description: There is a lot of talk these days about America as a multiracial democracy in crisis. This is often described as a clash between our highest ideals as Americans and darker realities that have emerged within our politics. However, this discourse often evades any discussion of the more complex underbelly of contradictions that "America" is. "America" is and has been many things at once, and fights over just who and what is "American" are nothing new. This seminar explores the many contradictions within American political and cultural identity and the various ways that the law and legal frameworks have attempted to reconcile those contradictions. In this seminar, we well read a selection of academic and popular analysis of this crisis against a backdrop of legal and political writings on American identity and pluralism. We will contrast the present discussions of America's struggles over minority rights, discrimination, and cultural pluralism with political theory and historical accounts on the development of American cultural identity. We will explore themes of race, culture, religion, culture, and colonialism. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 4:30 PM-6:30 PM on Oct. 8, Oct. 15, Oct. 22, Nov 5.

title: Discussion (1L): Environmental Democracy: Past, Present, and Future
description: The basic pillars of the U.S. environmental democracy movement that took root in the 1960s and 1970s are transparency, public participation, and accountability. The implementation of these three principles through various laws and regulations transformed environmental decisionmaking and significantly improved the physical environment. At the same time, however, it arguably added more time, more process, and more cost to the permitting of projects and the decisions of regulators. In response, there has now developed a growing backlash by academics like University of Michigan legal scholar Nicholas Bagley and Stanford political scientist Francis Fukuyama, amplified by such public intellectuals as Ezra Klein, Derek Thompson, and Marc Dunkelman. Whatever one calls these critiques -- Vetocracy, the Abundance Agenda, and Supply-side Progressivism are a few of the catchy labels -- they cohere around the notion that our well-intentioned environmental laws and regulations have created a world of scarcity by hobbling society's ability to build the future we want. To achieve a fully-decarbonized economy and harvest the bountiful amenities that will make our lives better, richer, and easier, the critics argue, we need to unshackle the forces of growth and innovation from "paperwork and procedure and hearings and disclosure demands and lawsuits." But where does that leave the equally powerful ideal of environmental democracy, especially at a time when populism is ascendent on both the left and the right? In this discussion seminar, we will interrogate these ideas and critiques and explore whether and how we might find a viable path forward. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned material, and active participation. Class meets: 5:30 PM-7:30 PM on Sept. 14, Sept. 28, Oct. 12, Oct. 26.

title: Discussion (1L): Excursions in Criminal Law
description: This discussion seminar will focus on four topics/cases surrounding the impact of criminal law on society. The probable content will likely be as follows: One session will likely focus on The Central Park 5 case where five youths were wrongfully convicted in 1990 of the assault in Central Park on a jogger. They were ultimately exonerated in 2002, but the racial overtones associated with their conviction still lingers. The second session will likely focus on the weaponization of the Department of Justice as a political matter and what it implies for the rule of law. The third session will likely discuss the use of solitary confinement and its justification and consequence to those incarcerated and subjected to its application. The fourth will likely discuss the case pending in the Supreme Court of California concerning racial disparity in the application of California's Three Strikes Law. We will likely have guests who are intimately involved in these matters join us for one or more sessions. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 4:30 PM-6:30 PM on Sept. 15, Sept. 29, Oct. 13, Oct. 27.

title: Discussion (1L): Free Speech and Internet Platforms
description: This discussion seminar will examine the ways that internet and social media platforms regulate speech. We will explore the policies and case studies related to hate speech, incitement, indecency, disinformation, and child protection. Readings will include rulings from the Facebook Oversight Board as well as community standards from several other internet companies. We will be joined by the Global Head of Trust and Safety for YouTube at most sessions. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 5:15 PM-7:15 PM on Sept. 28, Oct. 5, Oct. 12, Oct. 19.

title: Discussion (1L): Government Hiring and Firing
description: This discussion seminar will address the hiring and firing of federal agency officials, at the leadership level and below. It will draw from recent court decisions and ongoing litigation as well as from historical, social science, and policy materials. We will discuss some initiatives of the current Administration (including Schedule P/C, RIFs, and DOGE) and consider how they compare to the Clinton Administration's Reinventing Government efforts (including RIFs) and other past personnel initiatives. We will also focus on how to build talent in the government in a highly partisan environment and with increasing AI use, with special attention to lawyers. Commentators have long lamented the slow pace of hiring (at all tiers), the difficulty dealing with poor performers, and the lack of young people interested in pursuing a government career. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 4:15 PM-6:15 PM on Sept. 16, Sept. 30, Oct. 14, Oct. 28.

title: Discussion (1L): Is the Market Fair? Technology, Access, and the Law of Modern Finance
description: "Rigged." "Unfair." "Fixed." We might reach for these words when we think about financial markets, but what would it actually mean for a market to be fair? In this discussion seminar we will press that question in three arenas where law, technology, and finance collide. First, who gets to invest: the rule that you must be wealthy to buy into startups, and the new world of crypto, tokenized shares, and prediction markets that promises to get around it. Second, whether the prices in our stock exchanges are truly fair and transparent in an age of payment-for-order-flow, "free" trading with a purported single "best price" that may be neither best nor even knowable. Third, who gets to raise capital, from founders shut out by the affinity networks of venture capital to borrowers protected -- or not -- by fair- lending law. Throughout, we will confront a choice every lawyer eventually faces: do we pursue fairness by guaranteeing fair process and open access, or by dictating fair outcomes? No background in finance or economics is assumed or expected. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 5:00 PM-7:00 PM on Sept. 29, Oct. 13, Oct. 27, Nov 17.

title: Discussion (1L): On Tyranny: Xenophon's Dialogue and Leo Strauss's Commentary
description: Xenophon's classic dialogue features a discussion between a poet and the tyrant of Syracuse about the nature of tyranny -- a topic of special interest and concern today. The ironic frame of the dialogue -- in which the tyrant criticizes and the poet ostensibly defends tyranny -- make it especially engaging. The published version of the dialogue we will be using (Leo Straus, On Tyranny), was prepared by Leo Strauss, one of the most challenging and controversial political theorists of the 20th century, and is accompanied by an exchange between Strauss and Alexandre Kojève, a French political philosopher and author of Introduction to the Reading of Hegel. This work will serve as a springboard for our group to discuss the current state of freedom around the world and the rise of "post-liberalism" in the United States. The first session will be devoted largely to Xenophon's work, the second and third to Strauss and Kojève, and the fourth and final session to a free-wheeling discussion of debates today. We will begin each session with a home-cooked meal. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 6:30 PM-9:00 PM on Sept. 16, Oct. 14, Nov. 4, Nov 11.

title: Discussion (1L): Pharmaceutical Pricing and Access
description: Policymakers across the ideological spectrum describe the U.S. drug pricing system as "broken." But it is less clear how and why the system is broken, or what to do about it. Is the problem that patents delay competition? That Medicare pays the wrong way? That intermediaries distort the market? That fragile supply chains leave patients without needed medicines? That the system rewards the wrong innovations? In this discussion seminar, we will map the basic legal and policy architecture of pharmaceutical pricing and access in the United States and beyond. We will consider four sets of reform proposals: efforts to rein in drug patents, to let the government set prices or rely on prices from other markets, to address the middlemen and supply-chain failures in U.S. markets, and to expand access to medicines abroad. Our aim is to learn how lawyers and policymakers analyze the complex institutional tradeoffs these proposals present. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 6:00 PM-8:00 PM on Sept. 22, Oct. 6, Oct. 27, Nov 10.

title: Discussion (1L): Reading Jonathan Rauch, The Constitution of Knowledge
description: We will read and critically discuss Jonathan Rauch's The Constitution of Knowledge: A Defense of Truth (2021), which argues that human societies discover truth not through individual genius or pure reason, but rather through a vast, decentralized social system for adjudicating disagreement. Rauch calls this system the "constitution of knowledge," analogizing it to a political constitution. Just as the U.S. Constitution is designed to convert political conflict into peaceful collective decisions, the constitution of knowledge is a (largely unwritten) set of rules and institutions that convert countless fallible individual claims into reliable shared knowledge. And like our constitutional system, the knowledge system is vulnerable to disinformation and cancel culture. We will consider approaches to addressing these vulnerabilities within the constraints imposed by the first amendment. These issues are of special importance to anyone preparing to participate in the legal system, which has its own written and unwritten rules for getting at the truth. Dinner will be provided at the home of Paul and Iris Brest. You can purchase a hardcover or Kindle version of the book from Amazon. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 6:00 PM-8:00 PM on Sept. 24, Oct. 8, Oct. 22, Nov 5.

title: Discussion (1L): Reexamining Judicial Supremacy
description: Today, it is axiomatic that the Supreme Court has the final say on the meaning of the Constitution. But when and why did that view take hold? And is maintaining it a good thing for our civic and legal cultures? In this reading group, we will read Niko Bowie and Daphna Renan's provocative new book, Supremacy, and reconsider the history and present-day significance of the Supreme Court's role in interpreting the Constitution. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 6:00 PM-8:00 PM on Sept. 14, Sept. 28, Oct. 12, Oct. 26.

title: Discussion (1L): The Law and Politics of International Migration
description: This seminar will introduce students to the legal frameworks governing international migration, and a range of competing political theories of just borders. It will do so through the study of a series of contemporary and historical case studies of contentious international migrations, including the forced displacement of refugees. Elements used in grading: Full attendance, reading of assigned materials, and active participation. Class meets: 4:00 PM-6:00 PM on Oct. 1, Oct. 8, Oct. 29, Nov. 12.

title: Directed Research
description: Directed Research is an extraordinary opportunity for students beyond the first-year to research problems in any field of law. Directed research credit may not be awarded for work that duplicates the work of a course, clinic, or externship for which the student has registered. Directed research credit may be awarded for work that expands on work initially assigned in, or conceived during, a course, clinic, or externship, but only if the continued work represents a meaningful and substantial contribution to the already existing project, significantly beyond mere editing or polishing. If a student seeks to continue or expand on work that the student initiated previously (whether for a course, clinic, externship, or otherwise) a student must (1) share the initial work with the professor supervising the directed research, to the extent that work is non-privileged, and (2) obtain permission for the expansion from the instructor or supervisor who supervised the initial project. The final product must be embodied in a paper or other form of written work involving a substantial independent effort on the part of the student. A student must submit a detailed petition of at least 250 words, approved by the sponsoring faculty member, outlining his or her proposed project and demonstrating that the research is likely to result in a significant scholarly contribution. A student may petition for "Directed Research: Curricular Development" when the work involves assisting a Law School faculty member in developing concepts or materials for new and innovative law school courses. Both the supervising faculty member and the Associate Dean for Curriculum must approve petition for "Directed Research: Curricular Development." Students must meet with the instructor frequently for the purposes of report and guidance. Unit credit and grading basis (H/P/R/F or MP/R/F) is by arrangement up to the allowable limit. Students whose projects warrant more than four units should consider a Senior Thesis or the Research Track (See SLS Student Handbook for requirements and limitations). With the approval of the instructor, successful completion of a directed research project of two units or more may satisfy the JD writing requirement to the extent of one research writing course (R course). See Directed Research under Curricular Options in the SLS Student Handbook for requirements and limitations. Directed Research petitions are available on the Law School Registrar's Office website (see Forms and Petitions). Elements used in grading: Paper and as agreed to by instructor.

title: Senior Thesis
description: An opportunity for third-year students to engage in original research and to prepare a substantial written-work product on the scale of a law review article. The thesis topic should be chosen no later than two weeks after the beginning of the seventh term of law study and may be chosen during the sixth term. The topic is subject to the approval of the thesis supervisor, who may be any member of the Law School faculty under whose direction the student wishes to write the thesis and who is willing to assume the responsibility therefor. An oral defense of the thesis before members of the faculty, including the thesis supervisor, will be conducted late in the student's ninth academic term. Acceptance of the thesis for credit requires the approval of the thesis supervisor and one or more other members of the faculty who will be selected by the supervisor. Satisfactory completion of the senior thesis will satisfy graduation requirements to the extent of (a) 5 - 8 units of credit and (b) two research courses. The exact requirements for a senior thesis are in the discretion of the supervising faculty member. Unit credit and grading basis (H/P/R/F or MP/R/F) is by arrangement up to the allowable limit. Special Instructions: Two Research credits are possible. Elements used in grading: Paper and as agreed to by instructor.

title: Research Track
description: The Research Track is for students who wish to carry out a research project of a scope larger than that contemplated for a Senior Thesis. Research Track projects are to be supervised by two or more professors, at least one of whom must be a member of the Law School faculty. At least one faculty member in addition to the supervisors must read the written product of the research, and the student must defend the written work orally before the readers. Students will be admitted to Research Track only if they have a demonstrated capability for substantial independent research, and propose a significant and well-formulated project at the time of application. Special Instructions: Two Research credits are possible. Unit credit and grading basis (H/P/R/F or MP/R/F) is by arrangement up to the allowable limit. Elements used in grading: Paper and as agreed to by instructor.

title: Directed Professional Writing
description: Directed professional writing projects involve professional writing, such as motions, briefs, proposed legislation, and congressional testimony, undertaken with the assistance of --- and in collaboration with --- a faculty member. Directed professional writing credit is designed to allow a student, or a small group of students working together, to receive academic credit for their work tackling real-world problems. Only projects supervised by a member of the faculty (tenured, tenure- track, senior lecturer, or professor from practice) may qualify for Directed Professional Writing credit. It will not necessarily be appropriate to require each member of the team to write the number of pages that would be required for an individual directed research project earning the number of units that each team member will earn for the team project. The page length guidelines applicable to individual papers may be considered in determining the appropriate page length, but the faculty supervisor has discretion to make the final page-length determination. Students must meet with the instructor frequently for the purposes of report and guidance. Unit credit and grading basis (H/P/R/F or MP/R/F) is by arrangement up to the allowable limit. A petition will not be approved for work assigned or performed in a course, clinic, or externship for which the student has or will receive credit. Directed Professional Writing petitions are available on the Law School Registrar's Office website (see Forms and Petitions). Elements used in grading: As agreed to by instructor.

title: Policy Practicum: Roses Talk: Youth Participatory Action Research for Policy Impact
description: Efforts to elevate student voice in education decision-making have grown over the past decade--through state legislation, district governance structures, and school-based student groups. Leaders increasingly recognize that student perspectives are critical to improving outcomes amid persistent challenges in K-12 education. Yet existing student feedback mechanisms rarely capture the voices of students most impacted by those challenges--those whose experiences most clearly reveal where systems are failing. The Roses Talk Project (https://law.stanford.edu/stanford-center-for-racial-justice/projects/roses-talk-elevating-student- voice-in-policy-practice/) aims to counter this oversight through a novel research-practice partnership model that draws on the unique experiences of marginalized students to shed new light on policies and practices that harm or support marginalized students to inform education decision-making. With around 25,000 students, SJUSD is the largest school district in Santa Clara County, the county where Stanford University is located. District leaders and administrators at Gunderson--a Title I high school in South San José--have identified a collective need to better understand how to support "at-promise" students (a positive reframing of "at-risk" that is reflected in California education law). Building on a successful pilot that resulted in a first-of-its-kind set of recommendations (https://law.stanford.edu/2026/02/24/roses-talk-san-jose-unified-rethinking-education-policy-through-at-promise-student-voices/) for SJUSD and Gunderson grounded in marginalized student voices, the next phase of the project aims to: (1) validate initial findings through additional data collection and engage in comparative analysis between Phase I and Phase II; (2) evaluate the implementation of Phase I policy recommendations for their effectiveness in responding to student input; and (3) develop evidence-based guidance for SJUSD and Gunderson on how to translate student insights into actionable policy and practice interventions in the near- and long-term. This course uniquely integrates Youth Participatory Action Research into Phase II of the project. Stanford students will not only conduct research about marginalized students but will do so alongside them. Beginning in fall quarter and leading into winter quarter, Gunderson students serving on the Promising Voices Student Advisory Board (PVSAB) will join the Stanford policy lab as co-researchers, participating in data collection, analysis, and policy development. This collaboration ensures that young people most affected by these policies are active in developing solutions and building research and policy skills that enable them to serve their community beyond the project. In turn, Stanford students are provided a distinctive opportunity to participate in community- engaged learning and research, apply technical skills and academic knowledge to real-world challenges, and contribute to positive educational outcomes for underserved students--while building genuine partnership. This policy lab is unique in that the course offers what few do: a chance to collaborate with the at- promise students it is meant to serve. TIMELINE AND EXPECTATIONS: The practicum spans three quarters. In fall, Stanford students will be introduced to rigorous qualitative research methods, develop an interview protocol, conduct individual interviews with at-promise Gunderson students, and analyze data using qualitative coding techniques. Preliminary findings will be synthesized and presented to SJUSD and Gunderson leadership for feedback. In late fall and into winter, Gunderson PVSAB students join the lab as co-researchers. Together, the team will conduct member-checking focus groups, integrate and compare findings across phases, and conduct policy and legal research to begin developing Phase II recommendations and a report outline. In spring, Stanford and Gunderson students will collaborate to draft the full Phase II report--incorporating expert peer review--and present their findings at a project convening for a broad stakeholder audience. The report will be finalized over the summer through a community feedback loop with Gunderson and SJUSD leadership. Please note that this timeline is subject to change. LOGISTICS: Students are strongly encouraged to commit to all three quarters. However, students who are only able to participate in fall and winter quarters will be considered. Fall and winter quarter labs are each 3 units. Spring quarter is variable at 1--3 units (and up to 5 for EDUC 309X) to accommodate continuing students and the shift toward report drafting and convening preparation. Class sessions will be held on Thursdays from 9:50--11:50 AM and travel arrangements to/from San José will be determined as needed among instructors and students. ENROLLMENT AND GRADING: This class is open to Stanford Law School students, Stanford Graduate School of Education students, and available for cross-registration for undergraduate and graduate students from across campus. We highly encourage students from outside of Law and Education to apply, particularly students from CSRE, DAAAS, and others. Ideal students will have strong research, writing, and analytical skills, oral communications skills, and a demonstrated commitment to improving educational outcomes for all students. Students will be working together in small teams. Grading will be based on attendance, class performance and participation, collaboration with peers, engagement with high school students, written assignments, and presentations. COURSE OBJECTIVES: (1) Center the voices of marginalized students in school and district decision-making; (2) develop essential qualitative, policy, and legal research skills and apply those skills to real-world educational challenges; (3) collaborate with peers, Gunderson PVSAB students, and instructors to engage in rigorous qualitative methodologies and craft evidence-based policy recommendations for improving student outcomes, culminating in a Phase II report that influences policies and practices at Gunderson and in SJUSD; and (4) promote diverse perspectives by challenging existing beliefs about marginalized students and their communities, encouraging open-mindedness, and fostering thought-provoking conversations about contentious issues that appreciate a wide range of viewpoints. CONSENT APPLICATION AND ADDITIONAL MATERIALS: To apply for this course, students must submit a resume and writing sample via email to Dionna Rangel at drangel@law.stanford.edu. Please indicate in your email whether you are applying for fall/winter quarters only, or fall/winter/spring quarters. You must also submit a Consent Application Form at https://law.stanford.edu/education/courses/consent-of-instructor-forms/. See the Consent Application Form for instructions. All application materials are due by Wednesday, September 9 at 11:59 pm.Cross-listed with Education (EDUC 309X).

title: Policy Practicum: Who Serves? The Selection of Jurors
description: A hallmark of American criminal justice and of American democracy is the right to be tried by a jury of one's peers. But American juries are unrepresentative, in many respects, of the broader public, and the reasons for this are understudied. In particular, the process through which a pool of potential jurors is assembled in the courthouse is shrouded in obscurity. Much discretion is given to county court administrators in deciding how the master jury list is created, excuses and disqualifications are applied, and accommodations are granted. The policies and practices of local court systems can influence whether and how jury lists truly represent a cross-section of the public. In this policy lab, students will review data the Stanford Criminal Justice Center has received from the California Judicial Council related to jury engagement and will conduct interviews with, and gather additional data from court personnel responsible for the creation and management of juries at the local level. The goal will be to assess variations and determine best practices with regard to master list generation, excuses and disqualifications, responses to non-appearance, juror support services, and ongoing monitoring of outcomes. Students will carry out research assignments, individually or in groups, make regular presentations on their progress, and contribute to a final report. Elements used in grading: Attendance, Performance, Class Participation, Written Assignments, Final Paper. Students interested in joining the lab should submit an application (resume, transcript, and one-page statement of interest and relevant experience) on the SLS Policy Lab portal (go to link SLS Registrar https://registrar.law.stanford.edu/) and by email to Debbie Mukamal (dmukamal@law.stanford.edu) by Friday, September 11 at 5:00 pm.

title: Policy Practicum: Policy Drivers To Accelerate the Clean Energy Transition
description: Summary. The U.S. has a decades-long history of using a variety of legal and policy tools to promote the development and deployment of solar, wind and other clean energy sources at the federal and state levels. Application of these pro-clean energy federal and state tools have changed energy market dynamics and spurred remarkable growth in clean energy throughout the U.S. Continued expansion of clean energy resources--accompanied by new investments in related storage and electrical transmission resources--is essential to reliably and cost-effectively meet growing electricity needs while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. This will not be easy. It will require learning from past clean energy legal and policy successes--and failures--and adjusting them to today's volatile mix of spiking energy prices; the siting and operation of controversial new data centers; increased antipathy to some forms of clean energy; and a balkanized and slow-to-change electricity regulatory system. The "Policy Drivers to Accelerate the Clean Energy Transition" Policy Lab will take on this task by undertaking a multi-disciplinary historical review and critique of clean energy outcomes achieved at the federal and state levels, with a special focus on outcomes generated in a handful of target states including California, Texas, and Florida. In addition to evaluating the relative success achieved by applying traditional legal and policy tools to spur the growth of clean energy at the state and federal level, the Policy Lab will explore potential legal and policy responses at the federal and state level (including through the lens of actions being taken in target states) to anti-clean energy headwinds, on-going concerns about slow siting and permitting processes, opposition to large new data centers, utility reforms, and grid modernization needs. Based on this analysis, the Policy Lab will develop a menu of refreshed, evidence-based energy legal and policy recommendations for federal and state policy-makers, opinion-leaders, and activists. Additional Background. Historic support for clean energy. For many years, Congress and successive Administrations have supported research to improve clean energy technology; issued tax credits to incentivize the manufacture and deployment of solar, wind, and other clean energy sources; established deployment targets for wind and solar projects on public lands and in federal waters; and provided loans, grants and other financial benefits to expand solar and wind development in the U.S. Likewise, many states have supported the build-out of clean energy projects by, among other things, enacting Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) that require utilities to procure a specified percentage of renewable energy for their customers; establishing state-wide goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions; adopting favorable siting and permitting processes for clean energy projects; and improving utilities' versatility and cost-effectiveness by increasing and maximizing the deployment of distributed energy assets, improving the grid, and better aligning utility investment incentives. Identifying and analyzing new clean energy deployment challenges and noteworthy new policy proposals. The general consensus favoring reforms in speeding up the siting and permitting of energy and other infrastructure projects is colliding with public anxiety and resentment about high energy bills; negativity around hyperscalers' push to build massive new data centers on an expedited basis--some with "bring your own power" provisos; and more generalized, ideology-based local opposition and bans on renewable energy projects. These countervailing trendlines are complicating the buildout of clean energy and related storage and transmission projects in many jurisdictions, leading to some pro-clean energy jurisdictions to consider new policy tools that are designed to assuage concerns and overcome ideological blockage of projects. Meanwhile, frustration with the utility industry's lack of innovation and misaligned investment incentives has triggered multiple policy initiatives by federal and state officials to more aggressively address unacceptable interconnection queues, data center deployment and integration issues, and overall grid modernization needs. These and other key emerging policy initiatives will be identified and analyzed alongside the learnings obtained from the Policy Lab's analysis of traditionally-applied policy levers that the federal government and states have deployed to increase clean energy deployment in the U.S. Based on this cross-disciplinary research and data, Policy Lab participants will prepare a report (or series of reports) that make(s) evidence-based energy policy recommendations for future action by federal and state policy-makers. The Policy Lab's workplan. The Policy Lab's workplan will include the following elements: (1) Identify and summarize relevant existing social science research regarding attitudes toward clean energy development; (2) Identify and analyze key clean energy policy learnings in a small group of target states by (a) gathering data on clean energy adoption in target states; and (b) gathering additional relevant information on target states and from existing social science research, augmented by interviews and surveys; (3) Conduct a landscape survey to identify communities in target states in which there appear to be "hot spots" of clean energy adoption or opposition; conduct an in-depth investigation into relevant hot spot communities; (4) Compiling these research results into a catalogue of historically-applied clean energy policy options--and their relative effectiveness--for consideration by federal and state leaders; (4) Identify and analyze noteworthy new policy proposals that have surfaced over the last two to three years to address opposition and increase deployment of clean energy, storage, and transmission resources, including grid modernization needs and utility sector reforms; and (6( Based on this cross-disciplinary research and data, prepare a report (or series of reports) that make(s) evidence-based pro-clean energy policy recommendations for future action by federal and state policy-makers; (7) Stanford will host a conference and amplify Policy Lab findings across multiple media platforms. Elements used in grading: Attendance, Performance, Class Participation, Written Assignments, Final Paper. CONSENT APPLICATION: Interested students should submit a Policy Lab application (go to link SLS Registrar https://registrar.law.stanford.edu/). Admitted students will be notified by email with a permission number to enroll in LAW 810M. Admitted students have the option to forward the email notification to Luci Herman (lherman@stanford.edu) for a permission number to enroll EBS 292 (instead of LAW 810M).

title: Policy Practicum: Reinvigorating the MPP at Stanford
description: Stanford offers excellent programs leading to an MA in Public Policy and a Master of Public Policy (MPP) <https://publicpolicy.stanford.edu/undergraduate/major>. Yet these programs do not attract as many students as might be expected. As the university becomes more interested in enhancing its impact on societal problem solving at scale, it is asking whether Stanford's current policy offerings are making full use of the breadth, creativity, and institutional capacity across the campus. With this in mind, Debra Satz and George Triantis, deans of the School of H&S and SLS respectively, have convened a group of faculty and senior fellows to discuss the possibilities for reinvigorating the MPP - not to create a new school at Stanford, but rather to serve as a key node that draws together existing hubs of policy- oriented teaching and research. The Policy Lab will play a role in this effort, asking questions such as: (1) Given recent developments in foundational social science, societal conditions, technology, and geopolitics, what is a sound core curriculum in public policy that is simultaneously attractive to a broad range of students and sufficiently rigorous to meet both Stanford's own standards and those of an external accrediting body? (2) For what careers should we prepare our MPP graduates? We should consider positions in state and local as well as national governments, the vast nonprofit sector, and also the growing need for policy and government- related expertise in the for-profit sector (e.g., corporations, law firms). What curricular changes do we need if we fully reflect the fact that people with expertise in public policy play important roles in a wide array of occupations? (3) Should the MPP program add concentrations that draw on the expertise of faculty in various departments? (4) What would be the demand for an enhanced MPP (a) among current undergraduates considering it as a co-term program and (b) among potential applicants from outside of Stanford? To address these questions we will examine enrollment trends and careers of graduates in Stanford's programs; examine peer institutions' MPP programs to learn what they treat as foundational courses, how they present themselves to applicants, and what career paths their students take; catalog Stanford University's many policy-oriented programs with an eye to involving them in this effort; identify core policy topics that would provide a foundational base of knowledge and level the field among students of different backgrounds; consider the opportunities for offering concentrations in fields ranging from data science to health policy to corporate governance. The Policy Lab invites students from other disciplines as well as Stanford Law students. Elements used in grading: Attendance, performance, class participation, research team participation, written assignments. CONSENT APPLICATION: Interested students should submit a Policy Lab application (go to link SLS Registrar https://registrar.law.stanford.edu/).

title: Policy Practicum: Future of Global Refugee and Migration Governance
description: The global rise in xenophobic and anti-immigrant politics is rapidly reconfiguring global, regional, and bilateral frameworks governing asylum and forced displacement. Civil society organizations whose work seeks to protect the human rights of refugees and forced migrants report escalating disregard for binding international legal obligations. The purpose of this policy lab is to support a global coalition of these organizations in mapping emergent regimes such as third- country deportation agreements, and to consider strategies for transnational collaboration to ensure just futures in the governance of forced displacement. Our partner is the Global Strategic Litigation Counsel, for whom we will be conducting most of our research; we may, however, determine that some of our work is more suited to academic publications or as output beyond the immediate needs of the GSLC. Ideally, students will enroll in consecutive quarters to maintain continuity and to develop knowledge and expertise throughout the research process. In the fall term, we will undertake foundational scoping work with GSLC guidance, which will then determine the specific research pathways for the subsequent quarters. There will be multiple opportunities to meet with the partner to assess and discuss the legal and policy landscape challenges and identify the support that meets their needs. Students will participate in consultations with the partner, conduct multidisciplinary research, and collaborate to produce appropriate written output and oral presentations of their research findings. The work product will focus on policy memoranda and may also include draft pleadings and other submissions to global policy-making fora. After the term begins, students accepted into the course can transfer from section (01) into section (02), which meets the R requirement, with consent of the instructor. Elements used in grading: Attendance, performance, class participation, written assignments. CONSENT APPLICATION: Interested students should submit a Policy Lab application (go to link SLS Registrar https://registrar.law.stanford.edu/).

title: Policy Practicum: Leveling the Playing Field: Mitigating Developing Country Investment Treaty Risks
description: Many fragile and post-conflict nations--such as the 20 member states of the G7+ intergovernmental organization--are bound by older-generation Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) and International Investment Agreements (IIAs). While designed to attract foreign direct investment, these older texts frequently contain broad, vague, or obsolete provisions that expose least-developed nations to predatory litigation and costly Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) proceedings. Compounded by limited administrative capacity, states often face severe fiscal and legal risks, sometimes resulting in unfavorable arbitral awards rendered in default. In this Policy Lab, students will engage in international legal analysis and policy design activities by assisting selected G7+ member states in mapping their treaty networks, assessing systemic litigation vulnerabilities, and designing risk management strategies. In particular, students will: Analyze basic BIT and IIA provisions that pose high risks to state parties, including Fair and Equitable Treatment, Most-Favored-Nation, Expropriation, Umbrella Clauses, Stabilization Clauses, and Dispute Resolution provisions; Study case patterns of pending and concluded ISDS disputes involving fragile states, including identifying instances of default or non-participation by respondent states in international arbitration and the legal consequences of such non-participation; Examine legal mechanisms for treaty reform, assessing unilateral termination options, timeframes for treaties to remain in force ("sunset clauses"), and prospects for treaty amendment, where appropriate; Evaluate global investment treaty practices to identify modern provisions capable of protecting the state's right to engage in bona fide regulate and that are suitable for adaptation in fragile and conflict-affected contexts; Engage directly with G7+ leadership and diplomatic missions to share and provide advice on the results of the analysis performed in the Policy Lab. Elements used in grading: Attendance, performance, class participation, written assignments, and final paper.

title: Externship Companion Seminar
description: The practice of public interest law, whether at a nonprofit or government agency, requires an attorney to consider a host of issues distinct from those encountered in private practice. For example, how does a host's mission and vision of justice influence long-term and day-to-day strategic decisions? And, how is success measured when there are no obvious or easy things to count? This course will challenge students to apply these questions and others to what they learn from their respective externship experiences. Using reflection, class discussion, and simulation, this course will help students develop skills relevant to public interest practice. Students are required to write weekly reflection papers of 2 to 3 pages. Elements used in grading: Attendance; class participation; weekly reflection papers; and a final reflection paper.

title: Externship, Civil Law
description: Following approval of a student's application, the Civil Standard Externship Program (SEP) allows second and third year students to obtain academic credit for externing with select non-profit public interest, public policy, and government agencies for one quarter. The Civil SEP allows students to (a) gain experience in a field where a clinical course is not offered, or (b) pursue advanced work in an area of prior clinical practice. Students may extern for 20, 24, 30, or 34 hours per week. For a complete description of the Civil SEP, students should read the Externship Handbook, which is available from the Levin Center for Public Service and Public Interest Law or online at: http://www.law.stanford.edu/organizations/programs-and-centers/john-and-terry-levin-center-for-public-service-and-public- interest-law/externship-program-0 . Students wishing to enroll in an externship must meet various requirements that are set out in the Handbook. Students participating in the Civil SEP must also concurrently enroll in the Externship Companion Seminar (Law 881). An externship that otherwise meets the criteria for obtaining EL credit will be approved for EL credit when the field placement provides specialized experience complementary to a student's intended career path and comparable benefits cannot be obtained through other EL coursework at Stanford. Grading Elements used: Full participation and attendance, satisfactory evaluation by field placement supervisor, weekly reflection papers of two to three pages. .

title: Externship, Criminal Law
description: Following approval of a student's application, the Criminal Standard Externship Program (SEP) allows second and third year students to work for credit in criminal prosecutors' and defenders' offices for one quarter. Students may extern for 20, 24, 30, or 34 hours per week. For a complete description of the Criminal SEP, students should read the Externship Handbook, which is available from the Levin Center for Public Service and Public Interest Law or online at: http://www.law.stanford.edu/organizations/programs-and-centers/john-and-terry-levin-center-for-public-service-and-public-interest-law/externship-program-0 . Students wishing to enroll in an externship must meet various requirements that are set out in the Handbook. Students participating in the Criminal SEP must also concurrently enroll in the Externship Companion Seminar. An externship that otherwise meets the criteria for obtaining EL credit will be approved for EL credit when the field placement provides specialized experience complementary to a student's intended career path and comparable benefits cannot be obtained through other EL coursework at Stanford. Grading Elements used: Full participation and attendance, satisfactory evaluation by field placement supervisor, weekly reflection papers of two to three pages.

title: Externship, Special Circumstances
description: Following approval of a student's application, the Special Circumstances Externship Program (SCEP) allows second and third year students to work for credit for one quarter in non-profit public interest, public policy, and government agencies outside of the Bay Area. Standards for approval of a SCEP placement are similar to those for Directed Research proposals, although they are higher. Because there is a preference for local civil and criminal SEP placements (see Law 882 and Law 883), your SCEP proposal must explain (a) how it meets the goals of the externship program; and (b) why a similar project cannot be accomplished in one of the placements offered in the Bay Area. SCEP placements outside the Bay Area must be full-time. Students wishing to undertake a SCEP placement obtain the supervision of a faculty member who will oversee their externship and an accompanying tutorial. For a full description of the SCEP, students should read the Externship Handbook, which is available from the Levin Center for Public Service and Public Interest Law or online at: http://www.law.stanford.edu/organizations/programs-and-centers/john-and-terry-levin-center-for-public-service-and-public-interest-law/externship-program-0. Students wishing to enroll in an externship must meet the various requirements that are set out in the Handbook. An externship that otherwise meets the criteria for obtaining EL credit will be approved for EL credit when the field placement provides specialized experience complementary to a student's intended career path and comparable benefits cannot be obtained through other EL coursework at Stanford. Grading Elements used: Full participation and attendance, satisfactory evaluation by field placement supervisor, weekly reflection papers of three to five pages, and a final reflection paper of a length to be determined by your faculty supervisor.

title: Advanced Community Law Clinic
description: The Advanced Community Law Clinic offers law students who already participated in the Community Law Clinic as a full-time student the opportunity to work under supervision on additional and/or more advanced projects and cases in the clinic. Advanced Clinic students will also work with instructors to mentor students enrolled in the Community Law Clinic for the first time. Advanced students may arrange with the instructor to receive between three and seven units. No student may receive more than 27 overall clinical credits, however, during the course of the student's law school career. Special Instructions: Completion of the Community Law Clinic (Law 902A,B,C) is a prerequisite for the advanced clinic. Elements used in grading: Participation, reflective writing, and quality of case and project work.

title: Community Law Clinic: Clinical Practice
description: Located off-campus at a site accessible to low-income members of the communities adjacent to Stanford, the Community Law Clinic is the closest thing to a traditional legal services office within the Mills Legal Clinic. CLC is fundamentally a trial practice clinic, practicing in three distinct, but intertwined subject areas: (1) housing, (2) social security disability and public benefits, and (3) post-conviction relief. In addition to its off-campus location, hallmarks of the CLC practice include extensive client contact, civil litigation skills (motion practice, oral advocacy, fact investigation), and the fast pace that comes from being responsible for several matters at once. Each student represents clients in all three practice areas, allowing for a diverse experience with clients, opponents, and other system- actors. Students may also participate in larger policy and legislative efforts in the relevant subject matters. CLC work emphasizes students' embodying the role of a lawyer (as opposed to a policymaker, judge, or intern) and the development of communication, collaboration, time management, cultural humility and other skills necessary for any professional setting. After intensive training in weeks 1 and 2, the clinic curriculum includes two group seminar sessions per week and a once/week student-led case rounds session. CLC's off-campus location affords students the chance to explore local neighborhoods and the opportunity to form a close-knit and collaborative learning environment. Special Instructions: General Structure of Clinical Courses -- The Law School's clinical courses are offered on a full-time basis for 12 units. This allows students to immerse themselves in the professional experience without the need to balance clinical projects with other classes, exams and papers. Students enrolled in a clinic are not permitted to enroll in any other classes, seminars, directed research or other credit-yielding activities within the Law School or University during the quarter in which they are enrolled in a clinic. Nor are they allowed to serve as teaching assistants who are expected to attend a class on a regular basis. There is a limited exception for joint degree students who are required to take specific courses each quarter and who would be foreclosed from ever taking a clinic unless allowed to co-register. These exceptions are approved on a case-by-case basis. Clinic students are expected to work in their clinical office during most business hours Monday through Friday. Students are also expected to be available by e-mail or cell phone when elsewhere during those hours. Because students have no other courses (and hence no exams or papers), the clinical quarter begins the first day of classes and runs through the final day of the examination period. Students should not plan personal travel during the Monday to Friday work week without prior authorization from the clinical supervisor. The work during a typical week in a clinic is divided into three components. First, as they are for practicing attorneys, most of the hours of any week are taken up by work on client matters or case work (this time includes meetings with instructors to discuss the work). Again, as is the case for practicing lawyers, in some weeks these responsibilities demand time above and beyond "normal business hours." Second, students will spend approximately five-to-seven hours per week preparing for and participating in weekly discussions or other group work in their individual clinic (scheduling varies by clinic). Third over the course of the quarter each clinic student (with the exception of those enrolled in the Criminal Prosecution Clinic) is required to prepare for and attend a few inter-clinic group sessions. Students will be awarded three separate grades for their clinical quarter, each reflecting four units. The three grades are broken into the following categories: clinical practice; clinical methods; and clinical coursework. Grading is pursuant to the H/P system. Enrollment in a clinic is binding; once selected into a clinic to which he or she has applied, a student may not later drop the course except in limited and exceptional cases. Requests for withdrawal are processed through the formal petition and clinical faculty review process described in the clinic policy document posted on the SLS website. Students may not enroll in any clinic (full- time or advanced) which would result in them earning more than 27 clinical units during their law school career. The rules described here do not apply to advanced clinics for students who are continuing with a clinic in which they were previously enrolled. For information about advanced clinics, please see the course descriptions for those courses. For more information about clinic enrollment and operations, please see the clinic policy document posted on the SLS website. Elements used in grading: Clinical case/project work, seminar preparation and participation, attendance, reflection papers and project.

title: Advanced Criminal Defense Clinic
description: Students who have completed the Criminal Defense Clinic are eligible to apply for enrollment as returning students in Advanced Clinic. Advanced Clinic work may include: factual and legal analysis on Sixth Amendment violations of the right to a speedy trial, culminating in briefing and oral argument in the trial court; strategic advisement on techniques and strategies for direct examination, cross examination, admission of exhibits and Fourth Amendment constitutional legal analysis in moot hearings of active clinic motions; analysis of police reports and body camera footage for evidence of explicit or implicit bias exhibited by law enforcement officers in support of motions for violations of California's Racial Justice Act. During the Winter Quarter, students may advocate for the pre-trial liberty of incarcerated clients facing felony criminal charges in the Santa Clara County Superior Court, in collaboration with the Santa Clara County Public Defender's Office. This work may include in-custody client interviewing of incarcerated clients, in-court appearances at arraignments for initial bail determination for incarcerated clients, and the possibility of written and oral advocacy in a subsequent bail motion for clients who are not released at arraignment. This work provides Advanced Clinic students interested in a criminal defense practice a unique opportunity to engage in supported advocacy in the real-time high-volume setting of a criminal arraignment courtroom. Students may not enroll in any clinic (full-time or advanced) that would result in them earning more than 27 clinical units during their law school career.

title: Criminal Prosecution Clinic: Clinical Practice
description: The six students enrolled in the Criminal Prosecution Clinic advocate before the San Jose Superior Court under the guidance of Santa Clara County prosecutors and Professor George Fisher. Students formulate case strategy, identify and interview witnesses, and conduct evidentiary motions and preliminary hearings. Their cases concern thefts, burglaries, assaults, weapons possession, drunk driving, and a range of other crimes. Students offer testimony by police officers, crime victims, and other witnesses and cross-examine defense witnesses. Clinic students spend at least four full days a week--Mondays, Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays--at the D.A.'s office or in court. There generally will be two class sessions each week: a three-hour on-campus class on Wednesday mornings and a weekly lunch seminar at the D.A.'s office. Toward the beginning of the term, classes focus on skills training, including direct and cross-examination, admission of physical evidence, making and answering objections, and argument. Toward the end of the term, our classroom focus shifts to an examination and critique of the local mechanisms of criminal justice. Topics include the impact of race and class on the quality of justice; the institutional strengths and weaknesses of the actors in the system; prison conditions and prison reform; and the ethical issues that confront prosecutors and defense lawyers. Students typically tour San Quentin State Prison, the Central California Women's Facility in Chowchilla, and Hillcrest Juvenile Hall in San Mateo and have the option to spend an evening on a police ride-along. Students must submit regular written reflections on their experiences in and observations of the local criminal system. Their assigned cases often require written court filings. During most weeks students will meet one-on-one with the faculty supervisor. Evidence is a prerequisite. Courses in criminal procedure (investigation) and trial advocacy are strongly encouraged. Students will be awarded three separate grades, each reflecting four credits, for clinical practice, clinical methods, and clinical coursework. Elements used in grading include class attendance and participation, writing assignments, case preparation, and courtroom presentations and advocacy. Class attendance is mandatory. Grading is on the H/P system. Special Instructions: General Structure of Clinical Courses: All of the Law School's clinical courses, other than advanced clinics, are offered fulltime for twelve credits. This format allows students to immerse themselves in the professional experience without having to balance clinical projects with other classes, exams, and papers. Students enrolled in a clinic may not enroll in any other class, seminar, directed research, or other credit-yielding activity within the Law School or University during their clinical quarter. Nor are they allowed to serve as teaching assistants expected to attend a daytime class regularly. There is a limited exception for joint-degree students who are required to take specific courses each quarter and who would be foreclosed from taking a clinic unless allowed to co-register. These exceptions are approved case by case. The clinical quarter begins on the first day of classes and runs through the final day of exam period. Students should not plan personal travel during the Monday-to-Friday workweek without permission from onsite and faculty supervisors. Students are expected to be available by email or cellphone during workday hours Monday through Friday and are expected to devote at least thirty-five hours per week to various facets of this work. In some weeks casework may demand much longer hours. Enrollment in a clinic is binding: Once a student has applied to and been selected by a clinic, the student may not drop the course except in rare cases. Requests for withdrawal are processed through the formal petition and clinical faculty review process described in the clinic policy document posted on the SLS website. Students may not enroll in any clinic (fulltime or advanced) that would result in their earning more than twenty-seven clinical credits during their law school careers. For more general information about clinic enrollment and operations, please see the clinic policy document posted on the SLS website.

title: Advanced Environmental Law Clinic
description: The Advanced Environmental Law Clinic provides students who have already taken the Environmental Law Clinic the opportunity to continue intense individual project work. Advanced students often work on matters they worked on as full-time students, but they also have the chance to work on new matters and develop new skills. Advanced students work closely with supervising faculty on their designated projects and are expected to take increasing responsibility for managing their work and representing clients. In addition, advanced students often serve as mentors to less experienced full-time students and thereby receive training in basic team building and supervision. Advanced students may arrange to receive between two and seven units. No student may receive more than 27 total clinical units during the course of the student's law school career. title: Environmental Law Clinic: Clinical Practice
description: Students enrolled in the Clinic provide legal assistance to national, regional and grassroots non-profit organizations on a variety of environmental issues, with a focus on complex natural resource conservation and biodiversity matters at the interface of law, science and policy. Working under the direct supervision of practicing environmental attorneys, Clinic students help screen new matters and potential clients; formulate strategies; research and develop factual and legal issues; and prosecute administrative and litigation proceedings. During the term, students may meet with clients, opposing counsel or agency decision-makers; review and prepare administrative records; develop expert testimony; draft comment letters, petitions, pleading or briefs; and/or attend and present arguments in administrative and court hearings. In regular one-on-one meetings with supervising faculty, there is a heavy emphasis on learning how to write persuasively and present oral arguments. Indeed, in any given quarter, our students typically prepare a mix of state and federal, and trial and appellate, court pleadings, and because all of our hearings during the academic year are conducted by students, many students also have the opportunity to present oral argument in front of one or more judges. In addition, students participate in a regular seminar where we examine strategic, ethical and substantive issues arising out of the Clinic's work. The Clinic is a particularly good place to learn how to conduct effective legal research, marshal facts in support of legal arguments, and, above all, write well. We practice at all levels of state and federal court and before many local, state and federal administrative agencies. Our work involves extensive motions practice and brief writing, and often involves administrative petitions and policy papers. Our work is inherently cross-disciplinary.
